articles.title: CrowdStrike Uncovers New Agentic AI Campaigns
articles.context: Between May and August 2026, CrowdStrike Intelligence documented several incidents in which threat actors used AI not only to create tooling or artifacts, but to conduct agentic...
articles.full_text:
A new report from the CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations team details research into four previously unreported threat actors, each of whom left their offensive agent frameworks exposed via open directories. In doing so, they shared detailed insight into their use of AI agents and revealed how adversaries are quickly becoming more proficient in AI.

AI is changing the speed and scale of cyber operations. Counter Adversary Operations, which brings together the CrowdStrike Intelligence and CrowdStrike OverWatch teams, is closely watching. Between May and August 2026, CrowdStrike Intelligence documented several incidents in which threat actors used AI not only to create tooling or artifacts, but to conduct agentic campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

About the Adversaries

Below is a high-level overview of the threat actors behind these campaigns:

Threat Actor 1

A Spanish/English-speaking operator that has compromised at least 15 Argentina-based healthcare entities and exfiltrated credentials and medical records from at least one victim.

The threat actor ran a purpose-built autonomous penetration testing (pentesting) harness against Argentine healthcare organizations. They implemented a dual-agent architecture in which a “Supervisor” Claude Code agent selects the next task from a state machine (i.e., a predefined workflow of attack stages) and an “Executor” agent performs the task. This framework is derived from the open-source PentestGPT project, but the threat actor has rebuilt it with additional MCP servers, Python-based exploitation scripts, and skills.

Threat Actor 2

A Chinese-speaking operator with 20+ named global targets. They compromised government entities of two countries and targeted private sector entities in Brazil and the U.S., including entities in biotech, healthcare, food and beverage, retail, technology, and travel.

This threat actor primarily accessed Claude models via a China-based AI proxy service (aka a “transfer station”), and they built two pentesting harnesses that grant Claude Code varying levels of autonomy. One harness consists of a Python-based project that deterministically conducts reconnaissance and then asks an AI provider to choose among a preestablished set of possible actions that are deterministically routed to the appropriate agent. A different harness provides more agentic flexibility, allowing Claude Code to operate either as a single agent pursuing a target according to an elaborate standard operating procedure, or delegating actions to multiple specialist agents in parallel.

Threat Actor 3

The least sophisticated of the four in this report is an Indonesian-speaking actor that uses 819 skills (overwhelmingly sourced from public GitHub repositories, primarily claude-red1) without additional orchestration to enable Claude Code to conduct intrusion campaigns. In these campaigns, the threat actor instructs Claude Code to compromise a target and assumes the skills will offer sufficient guidance to ensure the intrusion succeeds. However, in the observed activity, the threat actor periodically had to intervene to overcome the model’s safety guardrails or to exhort Claude Code to keep trying to overcome a particular barrier.

Despite their limited grasp of security fundamentals, the threat actor still used Claude Code to compromise several Indonesian government domains, a government domain of another country, and several private-sector entities.

Threat Actor 4

Threat Actor 4 is a group of Russian-speaking individuals. They exfiltrated corporate client data from a U.S.-based customer relationship management vendor and compromised several private-sector SaaS and data center entities based in Russia, Kyrgyzstan, and the U.S., in addition to one government domain of another country.

This threat actor uses a single /pentest-setup slash command to task Claude Code with a seven-step workflow. This workflow provides guidance for enumerating the target environment, grants Claude Code near-total autonomy in selecting exploitation methods, defines a high-level post-remote code execution workflow, and provides explicit exfiltration instructions.

What This Means for Defenders

The four cases documented in this report likely demonstrate that agentic AI commoditizes baseline offensive cyber operations. This assessment is made with moderate confidence based on the included case studies, all of which showcase threat actors delegating operational decision-making across the kill chain to agentic AI. Working at machine speed, agentic AI can autonomously achieve objectives, often within an hour.

Findings from these cases likely support the following assessments:

Agentic AI-supported intrusions will almost certainly increase in volume and sophistication, an assessment made with high confidence based on threat actors’ rapid adoption of agentic AI, the effectiveness of the agentic AI-supported intrusions, the continuous improvements in AI models, and the proliferation of open-source offensive agent frameworks.2

Agentic AI will reduce barriers to effective intrusions as we expect over the next 12 months, some low-skill threat actors will likely use agentic AI to conduct campaigns at a level of effectiveness and scale previously only achievable by organized criminal groups or state-nexus actors.

Some threat actors will likely improve the OPSEC of their agentic intrusion campaigns over the next 12 months, an assessment made with moderate confidence based on AI development trends and trusted open-source reporting.

The team’s findings expand on how these adversaries weaponize AI coding assistants and enable long-term agentic operations using different methodologies. Download the full report for detailed case studies and guidance on how defenders can respond to this activity.

1 https[:]//github[.]com/SnailSploit/Claude-Red

2 https[:]//github[.]com/vxcontrol/pentagi

articles.title: CrowdStrike Achieves NCSC CIR Enhanced Level Assurance
articles.context: The time to patch is also shrinking: In the first half of 2026, 88% of observed exploitation of vulnerabilities with a public proof of concept happened within 48 hours of its...
articles.full_text:
Some cyber incidents leave no margin for error, whether that's an attack that interrupts energy, water, or financial services, or a breach that triggers reporting obligations in several jurisdictions within hours.

The UK National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) created the Enhanced Level of its Cyber Incident Response (CIR) scheme for incidents like these. It recognizes providers that meet rigorous standards for high-quality incident response, at the highest level of risk.

Today, CrowdStrike has been assured at the Enhanced Level of the NCSC CIR scheme, the highest level of incident response assurance the UK government offers.

This builds on the CIR Standard Level assurance we announced earlier this year and gives UK organizations independent, government-backed proof that CrowdStrike can respond when the stakes are highest.

As Adversaries Accelerate with AI, Defenders Must Keep Up

Europe remains a prime target. According to the CrowdStrike 2025 European Threat Landscape Report, 22% of all victims named on dedicated leak sites are based in Europe, making it the second most targeted region after North America.

AI is making the adversaries behind those attacks faster and more capable. Attacks by AI-enabled adversaries rose 89% year-over-year, and the fastest breakout time fell to just 27 seconds, according to the CrowdStrike 2026 Global Threat Report. The time to patch is also shrinking: In the first half of 2026, 88% of observed exploitation of vulnerabilities with a public proof of concept happened within 48 hours of its release, the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report found.

As the window to defend narrows, organizations need a response partner that has already proven it can operate at the highest level.

The Highest Bar, Independently Proven

Every NCSC-assured provider must meet rigorous standards for incident response quality, including core skills in digital forensics, network traffic inspection, and malware analysis. The Enhanced Level goes much further. Providers must demonstrate expertise against the most capable adversaries, across the largest and most complex environments, delivered to the highest standard of quality.

Table 1. NCSC CIR Enhanced Level requirements

Capability area

What Enhanced demands

How CrowdStrike delivers

Adversaries

Experience responding to advanced persistent threat (APT) attacks, not only cybercrime

CrowdStrike tracks more than 290 named adversaries, including nation-state groups, and applies that knowledge of their tradecraft to every investigation

Intelligence

Producing cyber threat intelligence and using it to drive the response

CrowdStrike was named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Cyberthreat Intelligence, and threat intelligence directly informs incident response as CrowdStrike responders work alongside CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations

Technical depth

Advanced malware analysis and endpoint detection

CrowdStrike delivers deep reverse engineering and forensic expertise, accelerated by AI tooling, with every finding validated by CrowdStrike responders

Scale

Log analysis across large enterprise estates

The CrowdStrike Falcon® platform deploys rapidly across complex estates, with visibility across endpoint, identity, cloud, SaaS, and AI systems

Organizational complexity

Incidents at multinational companies and regulated-sector organizations

Dedicated teams worldwide provide 24/7 investigation support in global and local languages

Stakeholders

Incidents involving external legal counsel and law enforcement

CrowdStrike collaborates closely with legal counsel, insurers, regulators, and law enforcement, backed by a network of more than 200 law firm and insurance partners

These capabilities are also why both Forrester and IDC have named CrowdStrike a Leader in incident response services.

Supporting the UK's Critical National Infrastructure

When an incident hits Critical National Infrastructure (CNI), the impact can quickly expand across the energy, water, transport, health, and financial services systems that millions of people depend on.

These are the environments where nation-state adversaries are most persistent and where response has to be fast, precise, and coordinated with regulators and government stakeholders. Enhanced Level assurance gives CNI operators independent confirmation that CrowdStrike has the expertise and quality to respond when it matters most.

"When the worst happens, organizations facing the most serious threats don't have time to wonder whether their response partner is up to the task. CIR Enhanced Level assurance answers that question before the first call is made. It independently validates what our team does every day: taking on sophisticated, increasingly AI-enabled adversaries, at scale, in environments where the stakes couldn't be higher. For our customers in the UK, it means they have a partner assured at the highest level the NCSC offers."

— Tom Etheridge, Chief Global Services Officer, CrowdStrike

Does Your Organization Need an Enhanced Provider?

The NCSC recommends that all UK organizations, from small businesses to central government, use an NCSC-assured provider when dealing with a cyber incident. For organizations where an incident could have the most serious consequences, it recommends the Enhanced Level. These include, but aren't limited to, organizations that are:

Part of CNI: Disruption can spread to the public and the essential services people rely on.

Part of UK central government: Incidents can carry national security implications.

A likely nation-state target: Nation-state adversaries are patient, well-resourced, and built to evade detection.

In a regulated sector: Breaches bring reporting obligations and regulatory scrutiny, so findings must hold up.

Operating in more than one country: Incidents cross borders, legal jurisdictions, and time zones, and response must do the same.

If any of these describe your organization, choose a response partner whose capability has been independently proven.

Don't Wait for a Breach to Choose a Responder

With a CrowdStrike Services Retainer, each organization gets guaranteed access to the CrowdStrike incident response team, assured at the NCSC's Enhanced Level, and a partner who already knows your environment before an adversary gets in.

Before an incident strikes, we help you:

Know where you're exposed: Gain visibility into exposures across endpoint, identity, cloud, SaaS, and AI systems, and prioritize what to fix first.

Strengthen detection and response: Improve how quickly your team detects and contains threats, whether you build that capability in-house or partner with CrowdStrike to deliver it.

Get ahead of the next attack: Test your defenses and response plans against real-world adversary techniques through tabletop exercises, compromise assessments, and red teaming.

Be ready before, during, and after a breach, with a partner assured at the NCSC's highest level. Talk to a CrowdStrike expert.

Experienced a breach? Get immediate help from our incident response team.

articles.title: U.S. Government Disrupts FAMOUS CHOLLIMA Operation with CrowdStrike Assistance
articles.context: Tune in to the Adversary Universe podcast, where CrowdStrike reveals the threat actors behind the latest cyberattacks
articles.full_text:
In late September 2026, CrowdStrike's Counter Adversary Operations team collaborated with the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to disrupt several laptop farms operating across the U.S. maintained by DPRK-nexus adversary FAMOUS CHOLLIMA to fraudulently employ operatives at American companies while concealing their true location and identity.

These laptop farms enabled FAMOUS CHOLLIMA operatives to pose as legitimate remote workers and siphon illicit wages back to their regime while maintaining persistent access to victim organizations. Working alongside the FBI, CrowdStrike’s threat intelligence into the adversary and their operations, and technical analysis helped make these disruptions possible.

This operation marks the beginning of a broader U.S. law enforcement effort to dismantle FAMOUS CHOLLIMA's U.S. infrastructure. CrowdStrike's Counter Adversary Operations team intends to remain an integral part of that effort.

FAMOUS CHOLLIMA’s Reliance on Laptop Farms

To conduct their employment fraud operations, FAMOUS CHOLLIMA operatives must first find a way to gain access to their employer-issued laptops. Because the adversary gains employment under fraudulent or stolen identities, shipping these laptops to their base of operations is not easily accomplished.

Instead, FAMOUS CHOLLIMA operatives employ a range of deception techniques during onboarding to direct their employer-provided hardware to laptop farm addresses. CrowdStrike OverWatch has observed operatives filing fraudulent police reports claiming a laptop was stolen to trigger replacement shipments to farm addresses; they rotate through residential addresses to obscure the final destination. Others claimed last-minute relocations to divert devices mid-shipment. In some cases, operatives secured roles through IT staffing firms, which allowed end-client devices to be quietly redirected to farm infrastructure without the staffing firm's knowledge.

Once at the farm, a facilitator installs a combination of hardware and software onto these laptops to enable remote access. CrowdStrike Overwatch has seen FAMOUS CHOLLIMA attempt to hide their use of these RMM tools, likely due to increased operational security following public reporting on their activity.

Since May 2026, FAMOUS CHOLLIMA has begun spoofing device hashes; for example, making a video capture card appear as a webcam. Most recently, CrowdStrike OverWatch observed FAMOUS CHOLLIMA using the same disguised device across multiple separate victim organizations, suggesting operatives are deliberately reusing device identifiers to evade detection. This demonstrates clear awareness of the indicators defenders are tracking. Network infrastructure within laptop farms was found sharing identifiers across multiple concurrent fake personas, a sign of the operation's scale and coordination.

Laptop farms are vital to FAMOUS CHOLLIMA's revenue-generating operations because they solve three problems the adversary cannot easily overcome from abroad: physical, financial, and legal.

Without a U.S.-based presence, FAMOUS CHOLLIMA’s operatives would be unable to receive and configure employer-provided hardware, defeat geolocation-based fraud controls, or navigate the identity verification systems that gatekeep legitimate employment. The laptop farm and its facilitators serve as a rented U.S. footprint: a physical address, a legal identity, and a mechanism to satisfy “know your client” regulations, which are part of financial institutions’ due diligence requirements.

While disrupting a laptop farm will likely only yield a limited impact on FAMOUS CHOLLIMA, centered mostly on the geolocation of the takedown, these operations send a clear signal to the adversary that law enforcement and CrowdStrike have visibility into their infrastructure and are actively tracking their movements.

CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations' Role in Identifying FAMOUS CHOLLIMA's Laptop Farm Infrastructure

Between April 2025 and June 2026, CrowdStrike's Counter Adversary Operations team identified personas, technical indicators, and U.S.-based computers used by the adversary to enable their fraudulent employment operations. By combining telemetry-driven observations with insights derived from targeted operations conducted by CrowdStrike Counter Adversary Operations, the team was able to uncover key personas and expose U.S.-based facilitator networks supporting the scheme.

CrowdStrike’s Counter Adversary Operations team continues to monitor customer networks to protect them from FAMOUS CHOLLIMA infiltration efforts and passes relevant information to law enforcement to help counter the adversary from multiple directions.

The dozens of victim organizations identified across the clusters disrupted in this operation span critical sectors including aerospace, energy, financial services, healthcare, cybersecurity, defense engineering, government technology, and consumer technology. This breadth reflects FAMOUS CHOLLIMA's sector-agnostic targeting posture, in which any organization offering remote employment provides an opportunity for revenue generation.

Conclusion

FAMOUS CHOLLIMA’s U.S. operations are ongoing. This disruption will likely slow FAMOUS CHOLLIMA's operations only in the immediate areas where the laptop farms were shut down and is unlikely to create long-lasting effects. The adversary will almost certainly continue to evolve their methods to evade law enforcement discovery and disruption.

This action by law enforcement sends a clear message to FAMOUS CHOLLIMA: Their infrastructure is visible, their movements are being tracked, and the cost of operating is rising.

Visibility alone is not enough. Disruption operations like this one are a critical part of raising that cost. They force the adversary to rebuild, relocate, and reinvest resources that would otherwise fund the regime's priorities. Every farm taken down is time and money FAMOUS CHOLLIMA cannot get back.

To that end, CrowdStrike’s Counter Adversary Operations team remains deeply committed to its partnership with law enforcement. FAMOUS CHOLLIMA has proven itself a persistent and adaptive adversary. But persistence cuts both ways. CrowdStrike’s Counter Adversary Operations team will continue to track their evolution, expose their infrastructure, and work with our partners to ensure every intrusion, every fraudulent hire, and every stolen paycheck carries real consequences.

Recommendations

While maintaining a list of known FAMOUS CHOLLIMA personas and indicators is useful, these are highly transient. When assessing potential hires’ proof of identity, run a standard background check and look for the following indicators:

Reuse of phone numbers, email addresses, bank accounts, or content such as resume text or website copy across multiple online profiles

Use of remote computing applications such as Astrill VPN, AnyDesk, OBS Studio, or PiKVM

Discrepancies between appearance on video and on identity documents

Logins to multiple locations during time zones that do not match the reported location

Discrepancies between the residential address and shipping address

Use of other FAMOUS CHOLLIMA personas as job references

Online connections to FAMOUS CHOLLIMA personas, including GitHub followers or LinkedIn connections

Accounts at any bank that allows account holders to create multiple virtual account numbers and easily convert funds to cryptocurrency

New public profiles on LinkedIn, Twitter, GitHub, or freelancer platforms
